context: Al-Insan is placed in Madinah in the common ordering, though early authorities differ, some holding it Makkan and some only partly so, a disagreement old enough to report rather than settle. Its listeners already fast, keep vows and stand at night rather than argue about resurrection. A much repeated account attaches verses eight and nine to one household that gave away its evening meal three nights running, but hadith critics have questioned its chains.

Those proportions follow from the audience. Refusal takes a single verse, chains and shackles and a blaze, while more than fifteen go to the garden. It is written for people currently going without, and closes by turning to the Prophet ﷺ with instructions about patience and the night.
name_story: The surah opens by asking whether there came upon man a stretch of time in which he was not a thing worth mentioning, and takes its name from that line. Two further names come from the same verse: Ad-Dahr, for the long span of time, and Hal Ata, from the opening words. All three make one claim, that the subject is man from before he existed.

movements.note: Man is set before his own beginning, then made from a mingled drop and given hearing and sight so that he can be tested. Verse three states the arrangement: the road shown, the response left open.

One verse covers chains, shackles and a blaze; the rest belongs to the righteous. They kept their vows, feared a day whose evil spreads wide, and gave food they still wanted to a needy person, an orphan and a captive, refusing repayment and thanks.

Couches, no sun and no bitter cold, shade overhead, fruit within reach, a cup mixed with ginger from a spring named Salsabil, green silk, a purifying drink. It ends by telling them their effort has been appreciated.

The Qur'an was sent down in stages, and the Prophet ﷺ is told to wait for his Lord's decision, to obey neither sinner nor ingrate, to remember his Lord's name at both ends of the day and to prostrate in the night.

Those opposite get one line: they love what comes quickly and leave a heavy day behind them. Their frames were knit together by Allah and could be exchanged for others like them, and no one wills except as Allah wills.

themes.d: Verse two gives the reason for hearing and sight before anything is asked of anyone. Accountability follows from what a creature was given, not imposed on one who lacked it.
The road is shown once and the outcome is not forced. Both possibilities are stated in one breath, and the surah then shows what each looks like across a life.
The givers in verse nine speak, and what they say is a refusal: no reward from you, no thanks. Removing every human return is what makes the act count.
Enduring a sinner's pressure in public is paired with prostrating in the dark where nobody sees. Consecutive verses carry both, each expected to hold the other up.

heart: Every verse of Al-Insan ends on the same long vowel, thirty-one times without a break, so it is easier to hear as one continuous thing than as separate statements. Read slowly, the garden section stops being a list: a cup, a cushion, shade, fruit brought close enough to take, each the opposite of what the people in verses seven to ten were going without.

The line doing the most work is short and easy to pass over. We feed you only for the face of Allah, we want no reward from you and no thanks. It arrives as a quotation, something the givers said rather than were told to say.

passages.why: The question about the time when a person was not a thing worth mentioning. It fixes a starting point no argument can move, since nobody remembers being nothing.
Guidance given, then two words: grateful or ungrateful. The road and the freedom to refuse it, stated in one line with neither possibility softened.
Food given while it was still wanted, to a needy person, an orphan and a captive, then the givers refusing thanks. The captive is the detail readers notice, having no claim on them.
Remembrance at both ends of the day and prostration in the night, the surah's only sustained instruction about practice, addressed first to the Prophet ﷺ.

connections.why: As-Sajdah is its pair in the dawn prayer on Friday by the Prophet's ﷺ own practice, so the two were meant to be heard one after the other.
The two stand side by side and share a sentence: Al-Qiyamah says the deniers love the immediate and leave the Hereafter, Al-Insan that its opponents leave a heavy day behind them.

virtue.text: Abu Hurayrah reported that the Prophet ﷺ used to recite Alif Lam Mim Tanzil, meaning Surah As-Sajdah, and Hal Ata 'ala al-Insan, meaning this surah, in the dawn prayer on Friday, and that report is in Sahih al-Bukhari 891. The same practice is reported from Ibn Abbas in Sahih Muslim. It establishes a settled practice at a fixed time in the week rather than promising a reward for reciting the surah at other times.
virtue.src: Bukhari 891; and from Ibn Abbas in Muslim
